Block 6 says large dot products push softmax into regions with tiny gradients and that additive attention beat unscaled dot-product attention at large d_k. The widget in block 8 adds that with unit-variance components the raw scores spread out as d_k grows, so the weights collapse onto one key.
answers.answer: When d_k is large, raw dot products of random unit-variance vectors grow large and spread widely. Softmax then saturates, putting nearly all weight on one key, and its gradients become tiny, so learning stalls. Dividing by √d_k keeps scores on a similar scale at any dimension, so the softmax stays responsive and trainable.

Block 15's Table 1 gives self-attention O(1) sequential operations versus O(n) for recurrence. It also says per-layer cost is lower only when n<d, so the colleague's 'whatever the input' is wrong and parallelism is the better account.

Block 2 names the cost as reduced effective resolution from averaging. Block 10 explains how separate heads attend in different subspaces, and block 22's Table 3 (A) shows one head scoring 24.9 against 25.8 for the best setting.
answers.answer: The cost is reduced effective resolution: each attention output is a weighted average of positions, so distinct pieces of information, such as a verb's subject and object, get blurred together. Multi-head attention runs several smaller attentions in parallel, each with its own learned projections, so different heads can focus on different relations in different subspaces. Evidence: in Table 3, a single head scored 24.9 BLEU, 0.9 below the best multi-head setting (25.8), at equal computation.
